7709.t: From μελῳδός (melōidós, “musical”) + -ία (-ía), from μέλος (mélos) "musical phrase" + ᾠδή (ōidḗ), contracted form of ἀοιδή (aoidḗ) "song".

7798.t: Traditionally (Pokorny, Vasmer, etc.) grouped with Proto-Slavic *myslь (“idea, thought”), Lithuanian mausti (“to long for”), Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (maudjan, “to remind”), Sanskrit मिथ्या (mithyā, “false, spurious, illusory”), all of which point to…

7782.t: From μαθ- (măth-, root of μανθάνω (mănthắnō, “to learn”)) + -μα (-mă, result noun suffix).

7774.t: From μύστης (mŭ́stēs, “one who has been initiated”) + -ικός (-ĭkós).

7737.t: From μετέχω (metékhō, “to take part”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).

7797.t: From μαγ- (mag-) (the root of μάσσω (mássō, “to knead”)) + -ια (-ia), the former component from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵ- (“to knead”).

7783.t: Back formed from the onomatopoeic baby-talk μάμμα (mắmmă).

7780.t: Derived from μόνος (mónos, “single, only”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “ruler, leader”).

7794.t: According to Beekes, both the variants listed in the alternative forms section suggest a Pre-Greek origin.

7781.t: The word recalls μῖσος (mîsos, “hatred”) but remains without certain etymology. Pokorny compares Irish mosach (“shaggy, bristly”), Low German mussig (“dirty”) and Russian му́слить (múslitʹ, “to suck, beslaver”).

7711.t: From the same Pre-Greek source of βαμβραδών (bămbrădṓn, kind of sprat) and βεβράδα (bebrắdā, kind of smelt).

7729.t: μετα- (meta-) + ἀνίστημι (anístēmi), itself from ἀνα- (ana-) + ἵστημι (hístēmi).

7777.t: The following is paraphrased from the entry by Beekes in his Etymological Dictionary of Greek: Beekes finds obvious to take this verb as an intensive deverbative, suggesting that the rare forms μωκός (mōkós) and μῶκος (môkos) are actually back-formations.

7795.t: From μυέω (muéō, “to initiate into mysteries”), from μύω (mū́ō, “to shut”).
